knitr::opts_chunk$set(

# helpers for numbers reported in the text
num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  format(signif(as.numeric(x), digits), scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
}
dec <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(as.numeric(x), digits = digits, format = "f")
below <- function(x, thresh) {
  if (all(is.finite(unlist(x))) && all(unlist(x) < thresh)) "below" else "not below"
}

# Overview

`stats2data` simulates raw datasets whose summary statistics match reported
summary statistics (the *targets*). Each module defines an objective, the
discrepancy between the summary statistics of a candidate dataset and the
targets, and minimizes it with simulated annealing. A run stops once the best
objective value falls below the convergence threshold `thresh` or once the
iteration budget is spent. In this vignette, a run whose best objective value
is below `thresh` is called *converged*.

Convergence is a statement about the optimization only, that is, the simulated
summary statistics reproduce the targets to within `thresh`. Many different
datasets share the same summary statistics, and a simulated dataset is one of
them. The results below are therefore described in terms of the optimization
objective values, target-vs-simulated differences, run-to-run variability.

The vignette works through four examples:

1. the **Descriptives module** (`optim_vec()`), using summary statistics of a
   simulated dataset with continuous and integer variables;
2. the **ANOVA module** (`optim_aov()`), using the reported cell means and
   F-statistics of Reynolds and Besner (2008);
3. the **MLR module** (`optim_mlr()`), using the reported descriptives,
   correlations, and regression estimates of Bardwell et al. (2003, 2007);
4. the **parallel workflow** (`parallel_optim()`), using the MLR example.

Across the examples, the following functions are demonstrated:

* the optimization functions `optim_vec()`, `optim_aov()`, `optim_mlr()`, and
  `parallel_optim()`, and the refinement step `hill_climb()`;
* the GRIM check `check_grim()`;
* the inspection methods `print()`, `summary()`, `get_stats()`, `get_rmse()`,
  and `coef()`;
* the plotting functions `plot_convergence()`, `plot_cooling()`, `plot_fit()`,
  `plot_stability()`, and the `plot()` methods;
* the Shiny interface `run_app()`.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# release version from CRAN
install.packages("stats2data")

# development version from GitHub
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("sebastian-lortz/stats2data")
```

## Setup

```{r load}
library(stats2data)
library(ggplot2)
```

# 1. Descriptives module: simulated example

`optim_vec()` simulates one vector per variable that reproduces a target mean
and SD within given bounds. To illustrate its use, the targets are computed
from a small simulated dataset with two continuous variables and one
integer-valued variable.

## 1.1 Encoding the targets

```{r vec-source}
set.seed(2026)
N <- 150
example_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(N, mean = 100, sd = 15),           # continuous, symmetric
  x2 = rgamma(N, shape = 2, scale = 3),         # continuous, right-skewed
  x3 = rbinom(N, size = 20, prob = 0.3)         # integer-valued
)
```

The targets are the means and SDs rounded to two decimals, as they would
typically be reported. The bounds are the observed minimum and maximum,
rounded outward:

```{r vec-targets}
target_mean <- round(sapply(example_data, mean), 2)
target_sd   <- round(sapply(example_data, sd), 2)
range       <- rbind(lower = floor(sapply(example_data, min)),
                     upper = ceiling(sapply(example_data, max)))
integer     <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)

target_mean
target_sd
range
```

`range` holds one column of lower and upper bounds per variable; a vector of
length two applies the same bounds to all variables. `integer` marks which
variables are integer-valued.

## 1.2 GRIM check

For integer-valued data, not every mean is attainable: the sum of `N`
integers divided by `N` can only take values on a grid of width `1 / N`. The
GRIM test (Brown & Heathers, 2017) checks whether a reported mean, rounded to
`decimals`, lies on that grid:

```{r vec-grim}
check_grim(n = N, target_mean = target_mean[["x3"]], decimals = 2)
```

For a mean that fails, `grim_mean` returns the nearest attainable mean
(hypothetical values):

```{r vec-grim-fail}
check_grim(n = 7, target_mean = 3.45, decimals = 2)
```

## 1.3 Running the optimizer

For continuous variables, `optim_vec()` starts from a vector whose mean lies
within `thresh` of the target mean and anneals the values toward the target
SD; the moves keep the mean fixed. For integer variables, it draws a
distribution from SPRITE (Heathers et al., 2018) via `rsprite2` whose mean and
SD match the targets at the number of decimals given by `sprite_prec`. The
objective of each variable is the absolute difference between its simulated
and target SD.

Both statistics are given to two decimals, so `sprite_prec = c(2, 2)`, and
`thresh = 0.005` is set to half a unit of the last decimal (both are the
defaults). The remaining arguments are at their defaults (`max_iter = 5e5`,
`init_temp = 1e-3`, `cooling_rate = NULL`, i.e. `(max_iter - 10) / max_iter`,
`max_starts = 3`).

```{r vec-run, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
result_vec <- optim_vec(
  N           = N,
  target_mean = target_mean,
  target_sd   = target_sd,
  range       = range,
  integer     = integer,
  sprite_prec = c(2, 2),
  thresh      = 0.005
)
```

## 1.4 Inspecting the result

`print()` shows the sample size and the best objective value per variable:

```{r vec-print}
result_vec
```

The best objective values are
`r below(result_vec$best_objective, 0.005)` `thresh = 0.005` for all three
variables. `summary()` adds the target and simulated means and SDs and their
RMSEs; the largest absolute difference between a simulated and a target mean
is `r num(max(abs(get_stats(result_vec)$mean - target_mean)))`:

```{r vec-summary}
summary(result_vec)
```

`get_stats()` returns the simulated statistics and `get_rmse()` the RMSEs
between simulated and target statistics:

```{r vec-stats}
get_stats(result_vec)
get_rmse(result_vec)
```

If SPRITE finds no distribution for an integer variable, the reason is stored
per variable in `error_msgs` (`NULL` when SPRITE succeeded):

```{r vec-msgs}
result_vec$error_msgs
```

## 1.5 Diagnostics

`plot_convergence()` shows the best objective value across iterations. For a
`stats2data_vec` result, `run` selects the variable. `log_y = TRUE` uses a
logarithmic y axis, and the shaded band marks the region below `thresh`.

```{r vec-convergence, fig.alt = "Objective trajectory of the x1 variable."}
plot_convergence(result_vec, run = 1, log_y = TRUE)
```

The trajectory of `x1` has `r length(result_vec$track_objective[[1]])`
iterations. Integer variables are drawn by SPRITE without annealing, so their
trajectory consists of a single value.

`plot_cooling()` shows the temperature schedule implied by `init_temp`,
`cooling_rate`, and `max_iter`:

```{r vec-cooling, fig.alt = "Cooling schedule of the descriptives optimization."}
plot_cooling(result_vec)
```

## 1.6 Target vs. simulated statistics

`plot_fit()` plots the difference between simulated and target statistics.
With `standardised = FALSE`, the differences are on the original scale; the
shaded band marks `+/- thresh`. `order = "fit"` sorts the statistics by
absolute difference.

```{r vec-fit, fig.alt = "Simulated minus target means and SDs."}
plot_fit(result_vec, standardised = FALSE, order = "fit")
```

The same plots are available through `plot()`, with `which` selecting the
panel:

```{r vec-plot, eval = FALSE}
plot(result_vec)                    # plot_convergence()
plot(result_vec, which = "cooling") # plot_cooling()
plot(result_vec, which = "fit")     # plot_fit()
```

## 1.7 Simulated data

The simulated data are stored in `result_vec$data`, one column per variable:

```{r vec-data, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Distributions of the three simulated variables."}
data_vec <- result_vec$data
head(data_vec)

data_long <- data.frame(
  variable = factor(rep(names(data_vec), each = nrow(data_vec)), levels = names(data_vec)),
  value    = unlist(data_vec, use.names = FALSE)
)
ggplot(data_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "grey60", colour = "grey20") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 2. ANOVA module: Reynolds and Besner (2008)

Reynolds and Besner (2008, Experiment 5) examined how contextual
predictability affects response times in word and nonword naming; the study
was among those replicated by the Open Science Collaboration (2015). To our
knowledge, the raw data are not publicly available.

## 2.1 Reported summary statistics

The study reports a 2 x 2 within-subjects design (`S = 16`) with four cell
means, indexed by stimulus type (`Factor1`) and switch condition (`Factor2`):
543, 536, 614, and 618 ms. It reports `MSE = 3070` for the `Factor1` effect,
`F(1, 15) = 30.5` (partial eta squared .670) for `Factor1`, and `F < 1` for
`Factor2` (.002) and the interaction (.015).

```{r aov-targets}
S   <- 16
mse <- 3070
target_group_means <- c(543, 536, 614, 618)
eta2   <- c(0.002, 0.015)  # Factor2, Factor1:Factor2
df_err <- S - 1
```

The numerator mean squares implied by the cell means of the balanced 2 x 2
within-subjects design are:

```{r aov-ms}
m_cell  <- matrix(target_group_means, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)  # rows: Factor1, cols: Factor2
m_grand <- mean(m_cell)
ms_f1   <- S * 2 * sum((rowMeans(m_cell) - m_grand)^2)
ms_f2   <- S * 2 * sum((colMeans(m_cell) - m_grand)^2)
ms_int  <- S * sum((m_cell - outer(rowMeans(m_cell), colMeans(m_cell), "+") + m_grand)^2)
c(ms_f1 = ms_f1, ms_f2 = ms_f2, ms_int = ms_int)
```

The reported `Factor1` statistics are consistent with each other: the implied
mean square divided by the reported `MSE` gives `F = 30.5`, and
`F / (F + df_error)` gives the reported partial eta squared of .670.

```{r aov-checks}
stopifnot(round(ms_f1 / mse, 1) == 30.5)
stopifnot(round(30.5 / (30.5 + df_err), 3) == 0.670)
```

For the two effects reported as `F < 1`, the F-statistics are set from the
reported partial eta squared via `F = eta^2 * df_error / (1 - eta^2)` (one
numerator degree of freedom). The modules require bounds for the outcome,
which the study does not report; the range of the reported cell means is
extended by four times `sqrt(MSE)`, the residual SD implied by the MSE, and
rounded outward. The summary statistics are encoded in one list of
`optim_aov()` arguments:

```{r aov-sumstats}
F_value_derived <- c(round(ms_f1 / mse, 1), round(eta2 * df_err / (1 - eta2), 3))

sumstats <- list(
  S                  = S,
  levels             = c(2, 2),
  factor_type        = c("within", "within"),
  formula            = "outcome ~ Factor1 * Factor2 + Error(ID / (Factor1 * Factor2))",
  integer            = FALSE,
  target_f_list      = list(
    effect  = c("Factor1", "Factor2", "Factor1:Factor2"),
    F_value = F_value_derived
  ),
  target_group_means = target_group_means,
  range              = c(floor(min(target_group_means) - 4 * sqrt(mse)),
                         ceiling(max(target_group_means) + 4 * sqrt(mse)))
)
sumstats$target_f_list$F_value
sumstats$range
```

`target_group_means` lists the cells with `Factor1` varying slowest (11, 12,
21, 22). Between-subjects and mixed designs are specified through
`factor_type` (and, for unequal group sizes, `subgroup_sizes`).

## 2.2 Simulating a dataset

`optim_aov()` is called with its default hyperparameters (`max_iter = 3e4`,
`thresh = 0.005`, `max_starts = 3`, `init_temp = 1e-3`, `cooling_rate = NULL`,
i.e. `(max_iter - 10) / max_iter`). The objective is the RMSE between the
simulated and target F-statistics.

```{r aov-run, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
result_aov <- do.call(optim_aov, sumstats)
```

## 2.3 Inspecting the output

```{r aov-print}
result_aov
```

```{r aov-summary}
summary(result_aov)
```

```{r aov-stats, include = FALSE}
stats_aov <- get_stats(result_aov)
rmse_aov  <- get_rmse(result_aov)
```

The simulated F-statistics are
`r paste(dec(stats_aov$F_value), collapse = ", ")` for `Factor1`,
`Factor2`, and `Factor1:Factor2` (targets 30.5, 0.030, 0.228); the F-statistic
RMSE is `r dec(rmse_aov$rmse_F)` and the cell-mean RMSE
`r num(rmse_aov$rmse_mean)`.

Before the annealing, `optim_aov()` may shift the target cell means by less
than `thresh` so that the means and F-statistics can be matched jointly. The
values used are stored in `adjusted_targets`:

```{r aov-adjusted}
result_aov$adjusted_targets
```

`get_stats()` returns the ANOVA table of the simulated data (fitted with
`afex`), the F-statistics, and the cell means; `get_rmse()` returns the two
RMSEs:

```{r aov-get}
get_stats(result_aov)
get_rmse(result_aov)
```

## 2.4 Diagnostics

The convergence trajectory (`first_iter = 1` skips the first iteration) and
the target-vs-simulated differences are obtained with:

```{r aov-convergence, fig.alt = "Objective trajectory of the ANOVA optimization on a log scale."}
plot_convergence(result_aov, first_iter = 1, log_y = TRUE)
```

```{r aov-fit, fig.alt = "Simulated minus target F-statistics."}
plot_fit(result_aov, standardised = FALSE)
```

`first_iter = 5000` plots from iteration 5000 onwards:

```{r aov-convergence-plain, eval = FALSE}
plot_convergence(result_aov, first_iter = 5000)
```

`plot_cooling()` shows the temperature schedule:

```{r aov-cooling, fig.alt = "Cooling schedule of the ANOVA optimization."}
plot_cooling(result_aov)
```

## 2.5 Simulated data

The data are stored in long format, one row per subject and cell. The
simulated observations lie within `range`; the second line checks whether any
observation equals one of the bounds:

```{r aov-data, fig.alt = "Simulated observations per cell with cell means."}
range(result_aov$data$outcome)
any(result_aov$data$outcome %in% sumstats$range)

data_aov <- result_aov$data
head(data_aov)
aggregate(outcome ~ Factor1 + Factor2, data = data_aov, FUN = mean)

ggplot(data_aov, aes(x = interaction(Factor1, Factor2, sep = "-"), y = outcome)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, colour = "grey40") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 4, size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Cell (Factor1-Factor2)", y = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Crosses mark the simulated cell means.

# 3. MLR module: Bardwell et al. (2003)

Bardwell et al. (2003) examined whether depressive symptoms or apnea
severity better predict fatigue in `N = 60` patients with obstructive sleep
apnea. This example uses the statistics reported there:

* means, SDs, and ranges from Table 1;
* the regression of fatigue on both apnea indices and depressive symptoms
  (Step 2) from Table 2;
* the correlations of the three predictors with fatigue from the Results
  section.

The same descriptives and coefficients are reprinted in Bardwell et al.
(2007), with ranges rounded to integers. The variables are the respiratory
disturbance index (`RDI`), the percentage of time with oxygen saturation
below 90% (`SaO2`), the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale
score (`CESD`), and the fatigue-inertia subscale of the Profile of Mood
States (`Fatigue`). To our knowledge, the raw data are not publicly
available.

## 3.1 Encoding the targets

```{r mlr-targets}
N           <- 60
target_mean <- c(RDI = 48.8, SaO2 = 17.3, CESD = 12.6, Fatigue = 10.8)
target_sd   <- c(RDI = 27.1, SaO2 = 20.1, CESD = 11.3, Fatigue = 7.3)
range       <- rbind(lower = c(RDI =  15, SaO2 =  0, CESD =  0, Fatigue =  0),
                     upper = c(RDI = 111, SaO2 = 80.9, CESD = 49, Fatigue = 28))
integer     <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
```

`RDI` and `SaO2` are treated as continuous, `CESD` and `Fatigue` as
integer-valued sum scores. Both means pass the GRIM check:

```{r mlr-grim}
vapply(c("CESD", "Fatigue"), function(v) {
  check_grim(n = N, target_mean = target_mean[[v]], decimals = 1)$test
}, logical(1))
```

`target_cor` holds the upper triangle of the correlation matrix of all
variables in `target_mean`, in the order of `target_mean`. Unreported
correlations are `NA` and excluded from the objective:

```{r mlr-cor}
vars    <- names(target_mean)
cor_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, 4, 4, dimnames = list(vars, vars))
cor_mat["RDI",  "Fatigue"] <- 0.11
cor_mat["SaO2", "Fatigue"] <- 0.20
cor_mat["CESD", "Fatigue"] <- 0.68
target_cor <- cor_mat[upper.tri(cor_mat)]
target_cor
```

`target_reg` and `target_se` follow the terms of `reg_equation`, intercept
first. The intercept is not reported; it is derived from the means and slopes
via `b0 = mean(Fatigue) - sum(b * mean(X))`, and its standard error is set to
`NA`:

```{r mlr-reg}
reg_equation <- "Fatigue ~ RDI + SaO2 + CESD"
b            <- c(RDI = 0.023, SaO2 = 0.008, CESD = 0.438)
b0           <- target_mean[["Fatigue"]] - sum(b * target_mean[names(b)])
target_reg   <- c("(Intercept)" = round(b0, 3), b)
target_se    <- c(NA, 0.034, 0.048, 0.066)
target_reg
```

The arguments are collected in one list, which is reused in Section 4:

```{r mlr-args}
args_mlr <- list(
  N            = N,
  target_mean  = target_mean,
  target_sd    = target_sd,
  range        = range,
  integer      = integer,
  sprite_prec  = c(1, 1),
  reg_equation = reg_equation,
  target_cor   = target_cor,
  target_reg   = target_reg,
  target_se    = target_se,
  thresh       = 0.005
)
```

## 3.2 Running the optimizer

`optim_mlr()` first calls `optim_vec()` to simulate the marginals and then
optimizes the values of the predictors with simulated annealing, followed by
hill climbing (`hill_climbs`). In the marginal step, `thresh` applies to the
continuous variables; the integer variables are matched by SPRITE to the
precision given by `sprite_prec`. The objective is
`weight * correlation error + (1 - weight) * regression error`, where the
regression error includes the standard errors when `target_se` is given.

The call uses `thresh = 0.005`, the default of `optim_mlr()`, which equals
half a unit of the second decimal, the precision of the reported
correlations. A stricter threshold would demand more precision than the
reported statistics carry. The coefficients are reported to three decimals,
but they depend on means and SDs rounded to one decimal. For example, the
rounding of the SDs of `Fatigue` (7.3) and `CESD` (11.3) alone leaves the
`CESD` slope (0.438) uncertain by about +/- 0.005.

All other arguments are `sprite_prec = c(1, 1)` (one reported decimal) and
the defaults (`weight = 0.5`, `max_iter = 1e5`, `max_starts = 3`,
`hill_climbs = 1e4`; `init_temp = NULL` is calibrated from the objective
changes of random swaps, `cooling_rate = NULL` is
`(max_iter - 10) / max_iter`).

```{r mlr-run, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
result_mlr <- do.call(optim_mlr, args_mlr)
```

## 3.3 Inspecting the result

```{r mlr-print}
result_mlr
```

The best objective value is `r num(result_mlr$best_objective)`, which is
`r below(result_mlr$best_objective, 0.001)` `thresh = 0.001`.

```{r mlr-summary}
summary(result_mlr)
```

`get_stats()` returns the fitted `lm` object, the coefficients, standard
errors, correlations (upper triangle in the order predictors, outcome), means,
and SDs of the simulated data. `coef()` refits the regression and returns the
coefficients:

```{r mlr-stats}
stats_mlr <- get_stats(result_mlr)
names(stats_mlr)
summary(stats_mlr$model)
coef(result_mlr)
get_rmse(result_mlr)
```

The marginal result of the internal `optim_vec()` call is stored in
`result_mlr$optim_vec` and supports the methods of Section 1:

```{r mlr-vec, fig.alt = "Simulated minus target means and SDs of the marginal step."}
get_rmse(result_mlr$optim_vec)
plot_fit(result_mlr$optim_vec, standardised = FALSE)
```

The RMSEs exceed `thresh` because `thresh` applies only to the continuous
variables `RDI` and `SaO2`, whereas the integer variables `CESD` and
`Fatigue` are matched by SPRITE only to the reported precision
(`sprite_prec = c(1, 1)`, i.e. within +/- 0.05).

## 3.4 Diagnostics

`plot_convergence()` shows the best objective value across the annealing
iterations; `first_iter` skips leading iterations, here the first 10%:

```{r mlr-convergence, fig.alt = "Objective trajectory of the MLR optimization."}
n_iter_mlr <- length(result_mlr$track_objective)
plot_convergence(result_mlr, log_y = TRUE, first_iter = floor(n_iter_mlr / 10))
```

With `ratio = TRUE`, the plot shows the ratio of the correlation error to the
regression error of the best candidate, with lines at its mean, median, and
final value (`show_mean`, `show_median`, `show_final`). A ratio above 1 means
that the correlation component is the larger of the two.

```{r mlr-ratio, fig.alt = "Ratio of correlation to regression error across iterations."}
plot_convergence(result_mlr, ratio = TRUE)
```

The final ratio is `r num(tail(result_mlr$track_objective_ratio, 1))`.

`plot_cooling()` uses the stored `init_temp` and `cooling_rate`, i.e. the
values calibrated during the run:

```{r mlr-cooling, fig.alt = "Cooling schedule of the MLR optimization."}
result_mlr$inputs$init_temp
plot_cooling(result_mlr)
```

## 3.5 Balancing the objective with `weight`

`weight` sets how much the correlation and the regression components
contribute to the objective. Objective values obtained with different
weights are on different scales and are not compared directly; the
unweighted RMSEs of `get_rmse()` are. The optimization is repeated with
`weight = 0.05`:

```{r mlr-weight, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
result_mlr_w05 <- do.call(optim_mlr, modifyList(args_mlr, list(weight = 0.05)))
```

```{r mlr-weight-compare}
rbind(
  "weight = 0.5" = unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr)),
  "weight = 0.05" = unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr_w05))
)
```

The table shows how the RMSEs of the correlations, coefficients, and standard
errors change with `weight` in this example. Which balance is preferable
depends on which targets matter most for the intended use of the data. The
remainder of this section continues with the `weight = 0.5` result.

## 3.6 Target vs. simulated statistics

```{r mlr-fit, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Simulated minus target coefficients, standard errors, and correlations."}
plot_fit(result_mlr, standardised = FALSE)
```

With the default `standardised = TRUE`, the differences are divided by the
target values (for targets of zero, the unstandardised difference is shown).
The `plot()` method offers the same panels, including `which = "ratio"`:

```{r mlr-plot, eval = FALSE}
plot(result_mlr, which = "fit")
plot(result_mlr, which = "ratio")
```

## 3.7 Refinement with `hill_climbs`

After the annealing, `optim_mlr()` refines the best candidate by hill
climbing: it repeatedly swaps pairs of values within a predictor column and
keeps a swap only if it lowers the objective. `hill_climbs` sets the number
of hill-climbing iterations (default `1e4`); `hill_climbs = 0` skips the
refinement. The optimization is repeated without refinement and with a
longer refinement. With the same seed, the annealing is identical across the
calls, so differences reflect the refinement only:

```{r mlr-hill, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
result_mlr_hc0 <- do.call(optim_mlr, modifyList(args_mlr, list(hill_climbs = 0)))

set.seed(2026)
result_mlr_hc5e4 <- do.call(optim_mlr, modifyList(args_mlr, list(hill_climbs = 5e4)))
```

```{r mlr-hill-compare}
rbind(
  "hill_climbs = 0"   = c(best_objective = result_mlr_hc0$best_objective,
                          unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr_hc0))),
  "hill_climbs = 1e4" = c(best_objective = result_mlr$best_objective,
                          unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr))),
  "hill_climbs = 5e4" = c(best_objective = result_mlr_hc5e4$best_objective,
                          unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr_hc5e4)))
)
```

`track_objective` covers the annealing only, so the effect of the refinement
is visible in `best_objective` and the RMSEs, not in `plot_convergence()`.

## 3.8 Simulated data

```{r mlr-data}
data_mlr <- result_mlr$data
head(data_mlr)
```

# 4. Parallel workflow: Bardwell et al. (2003)

Each run of an optimizer is subject to randomness, and many datasets share
the same summary statistics, so repeated runs return different datasets.
`parallel_optim()` repeats the optimization with the same arguments and
collects the runs; `seed` gives each run its own reproducible random-number
stream.

To keep the build time of this vignette short, the MLR optimization of
Section 3 is repeated 10 times with a reduced iteration budget and run
sequentially (`cores = 1`). For applied use, the default budget and more runs
are recommended.

```{r par-run, results = "hide"}
result_par <- parallel_optim(
  FUN   = optim_mlr, # MLR module
  args  = args_mlr,  # reported summary statistics
  runs  = 10,        # number of optimization runs
  cores = 1,         # number of parallel workers
  seed  = 2026       # reproducible seed per run
)
```

With `cores > 1`, `parallel_optim()` sets up a `future::multisession` plan
(Bengtsson, 2021) and restores any previous plan on exit. Because every run
has its own random-number stream derived from `seed`, the results do not
depend on `cores`:

```{r par-cores, eval = FALSE}
result_par <- parallel_optim(FUN = optim_mlr, args = args_mlr,
                             runs = 10, cores = 2, seed = 2026)
```

## 4.1 Inspecting the parallel output

```{r par-print}
result_par
```

```{r par-numbers, include = FALSE}
par_obj    <- vapply(result_par$results, function(r) r$best_objective, numeric(1))
par_thresh <- result_par$results[[1]]$inputs$thresh
par_rmse   <- get_rmse(result_par)
```

`r sum(par_obj < par_thresh)` of `r length(par_obj)` runs have a best
objective value below `thresh` = `r par_thresh`. Across runs, the best
objective values range from `r num(min(par_obj))` to `r num(max(par_obj))`.

`summary()` lists the best and mean objective values, the RMSE against the
targets and between runs, and the target statistics aggregated across runs:

```{r par-summary}
summary(result_par)
```

`get_stats()` aggregates each statistic across runs (mean, median, SD,
minimum, maximum):

```{r par-stats}
get_stats(result_par)
```

`get_rmse()` returns two RMSEs per run and metric: `target_rmse`, against
the targets, and `between_rmse`, against the across-run mean of the simulated
statistics. The per-run values are in `raw`:

```{r par-rmse}
par_rmse$target_rmse
par_rmse$between_rmse
```

The run-to-run RMSE quantifies how much the simulated statistics vary
between runs; it does not compare the runs with the original data.

## 4.2 Stability and fit across runs

`plot_stability()` shows the distributions of both RMSEs across runs,
faceted by metric:

```{r par-stability, fig.width = 7, fig.alt = "Run-to-run and to-target RMSE distributions across parallel runs."}
plot_stability(result_par)
```

`plot_fit()` shows the across-run mean difference per statistic, with error
bars for the across-run range (`error_type = "range"`, default) or
`mean +/- SD` (`error_type = "sd"`); dots mark the individual runs.

```{r par-fit, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Across-run differences between simulated and target statistics."}
plot_fit(result_par, standardised = FALSE)
```

```{r par-fit-sd, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Across-run differences with mean plus or minus SD error bars."}
plot_fit(result_par, standardised = FALSE, error_type = "sd")
```

`plot()` draws `plot_stability()` by default and `plot_fit()` with
`which = "fit"`:

```{r par-plot, eval = FALSE}
plot(result_par)
plot(result_par, which = "fit", standardised = FALSE)
```

## 4.3 Individual runs

The run with the lowest best objective value is stored in `best`; all runs
are in `results`. Both are ordinary `stats2data_mlr` objects and support the
methods of Section 3:

```{r par-best}
result_par$best
get_rmse(result_par$best)
head(result_par$results[[2]]$data)
```

## 4.4 Stopping at the first converged run

With `stop_conv = TRUE`, `parallel_optim()` stops launching runs once a run
has converged, i.e. its best objective value is below `thresh`. The example
repeats the MLR optimization of Section 3 with its full iteration budget:

```{r par-stop, results = "hide"}
result_first <- parallel_optim(
  FUN       = optim_mlr,
  args      = args_mlr,
  runs      = 10,
  cores     = 1,
  seed      = 2026,
  stop_conv = TRUE
)
```

```{r par-stop-print}
result_first
```

`r result_first$runs` of `r result_first$runs_requested` requested runs were
completed. With `cores > 1`, runs are dispatched in batches of `cores`, so a
whole batch completes before the check.

# Shiny interface

All three modules and the parallel workflow are also available in a
point-and-click interface:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_app()
```

The tabs *Descriptives*, *ANOVA*, and *Linear Regression* correspond to
`optim_vec()`, `optim_aov()`, and `optim_mlr()`. The inputs of each tab
correspond to the arguments of the function (the info icon of each input
names the argument), and setting *Number of Runs* above one calls
`parallel_optim()`. The results panel offers the plots and summaries shown in
this vignette. The *Download* button exports the result object, the simulated
data, and the R code of the function call, which reproduces the result in R.
